Why should you care about data analysis?

Think · Pair · Share

Only you can answer that. Purpose comes from doing something meaningful to you and useful to others.

Show that a problem existsGood analysis makes invisible problems visible, and helps others take them seriously.
Test solutionsDoes an intervention work? For everyone? With unintended consequences?
Evaluate evidence that affects livesWhether a drug works, or has serious side effects, shapes real decisions.
Question powerful claimsMarketing, policy and messaging often rely on selective statistics. What's missing? What's exaggerated?
Protect othersEspecially those with less power: from children targeted by unhealthy products to communities facing environmental harm.
Serve something biggerScience, public trust, health, biodiversity, fairness.

My role, your role, and how we'll work together

Becoming great data analysts

  • Everyone here can learn to think analytically and statistically.
  • I'll hold you to high standards, because I believe you can meet them. My job is to support you in reaching them.
  • Struggle is part of growth, not a sign of failure.
  • Stress before a challenge is normal: a faster heart and breathing are your body giving you more resources.

When did someone believe in you more than you believed in yourself? What happened?

High standards and wise feedback

“I'm giving you these comments because I have high standards and I know that you can meet them.”

“Wise feedback”: Cohen, G.L., Steele, C.M. & Ross, L.D. (1999). Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 25, 1302–1318.

  • Feedback will be honest and specific.
  • It comes from belief in your potential, not criticism of you as a person.
  • If it feels like criticism, try to reframe it as being challenged to grow.

This class is a safe space for you, and a challenging space for you.

AI assistants

Helpful, or harmful to your learning?

Vote, then tap

Your relationship with AI assistants

A strong relationship

The AI is a knowledgeable collaborator that complements your skills and supports your growth. You provide context, direction and critical judgement.

A poor relationship

You use output you don't understand, copying and pasting. Errors slip through, and your own skills stagnate.

The knowledge you bring is what makes the relationship good. So: minimise your use of AI during the course (and of the example solutions). Do the work, get the benefit.

The exam runs in the Safe Exam Browser: no generative AI at all, and no Copilot in RStudio. Practise without it.

Live data analysis

From question to answer in under an hour

  • It's a demonstration: a feel for what's involved.
  • You'll understand some of it, and not other parts. That's expected.
  • Keep notes about what you don't understand. Look for the answers as the course goes on.

The workflow in twelve steps

The first six steps all happen before any data are collected. That's Principle 1 in action.

    What should our question be?

    • Of interest to us, and of some importance.
    • Answerable with data we can collect, within our constraints.

    Do the reaction times of male and female students at the University of Zurich differ?

    “Male” and “female”: sex assigned at birth. Why care? Reaction times matter for safety (driving) and in sport (the start of a sprint).

      Expectation

      There has been quite a lot of research already.

      In general, males tend to have faster reaction times than females. So we expect the same for students at UZH.

      Curious? Lipps et al. (2011) looked at reaction times of sprinters at the Beijing Olympics (PLOS ONE).

        What graph will answer the question?

        Simulated data · not our data

        Sketch the graph before collecting data: box plots of reaction time (ms) for females and males.

          What statistical test? What assumptions?

          Response: reaction time (continuous). Explanatory variable: sex (two groups).

          A two-sample t-test compares the means of two groups.
          A natural first choice here. In later weeks you'll see it is a special case of a linear model.
          Its assumptions? (tap)
          Independent observations · values roughly normally distributed in each group · similar variances in the two groups.

            Selection of subjects

            Ideally a random sample of the population we want to draw conclusions about.

            Are you a random sample of… (tap)

            How subjects are selected limits who our conclusions apply to.

              Collecting data, and ethics

              How? An online test, and a form. Done: you just did it.

              Because these are data about people, we should think about ethics:

              Consent

              Taking part was voluntary.

              Anonymity

              No names. Could anyone be identified?

              Use and sharing

              For teaching, published for the practical.

                Data wrangling, visualisation, test

                Live in RStudio →

                Why a script in R, rather than pointing and clicking? It makes the analysis:

                EfficientConsistentRepeatableReliableReadableRobustPersistentSharableScalable

                That's Principle 4 in action.

                  Critical thinking, and reporting

                  How big is the difference?

                  Is it biologically relevant? (Principle 3)

                  How precise?

                  The confidence interval of the difference.

                  Other explanations?

                  Could something other than sex explain it?

                  To whom does it apply?

                  Given how the subjects were selected.

                  Report: a clear figure, and a sentence with the estimate, its uncertainty, and the test.

                  The four principles, in today's analysis

                  Principle 1

                  Question first

                  Question, expectation, graph and test, all decided before collecting data.

                  Principle 2

                  A suitable model

                  The t-test's assumptions. Later: counts, binary data, repeated measures.

                  Principle 3

                  Effect sizes

                  How big is the difference, how precise, does it matter?

                  Principle 4

                  Reproducible

                  A script anyone can re-run, on data that are shared.
